entry.title: Taste in Software
entry.content:
While restyling this site, I kept using phrases like this feels like too much, tone it down, and this does not look like my website anymore.

Those were not technical instructions. I could not always name the CSS responsible, but I could look at the result and decide that it was wrong for what I wanted. It made me ask: What is taste? What drives it? Is it technical or personal? Where do experience and creativity enter?

What is taste?

Taste is often described as knowing what is good, but that feels incomplete. Good according to whom, and good for what?

I think taste is the ability to notice differences, understand why they matter, and choose what fits a purpose. It is more than liking one colour, meal, design, or programming style over another.

A minimal website is not automatically tasteful. Removing everything is easy; knowing what must remain is harder. The same is true in software: fewer lines are not always better, and a clever abstraction is not always useful.

Taste is partly personal, but it is not random. It can be discussed, criticised, practised, and improved.

What drives taste?

Experience probably plays a large part, but experience is more than the number of years spent doing something. It is exposure, comparison, failure, feedback, and attention. You try something, see what happens, compare it with other work, and learn what you missed.

What looks like instinct from the outside may be compressed experience.

This is where taste becomes technical. A programmer may sense that an interface will become difficult to maintain. A designer may notice that a page has no hierarchy. A mechanic may hear that an engine is not behaving normally. Their judgment is supported by things they have seen, broken, and repaired before.

Technical knowledge gives taste something to work with. Taste helps decide how and when to use it.

The chef and the recipe

A recipe gives a chef ingredients, measurements, temperature, and cooking time. An experienced chef still tastes while cooking. They notice that an ingredient is stronger today, the pan is behaving differently, or the food needs acidity rather than more salt.

The chef does not even need to be the person who cooked the meal. By tasting it, they may be able to tell how it was prepared, where the process went wrong, or what is missing. They can judge the result because experience has given them a mental library of ingredients, techniques, and outcomes.

The recipe provides a path. The chef's taste guides the adjustments.

A blender, thermometer, or automatic mixer does not make the chef less skilled. The danger begins when someone can produce meals without ever learning to taste what they are producing. That feels close to the question we now face with AI.

Can models learn taste?

Fidel Etinosa, who reviewed an early draft of this article, challenged an assumption behind my question: if taste can be taught, why could a model not learn it too?

I think that is possible. Reasoning models are still young, so it would be careless to treat their current limitations as permanent ones.

But if models can learn taste, why do they not already seem to have it? Their training data contains excellent code, design, writing, and criticism. It also contains mediocre work and conflicting ideas about what good means.

The model's source code does not contain taste directly; it defines the process through which patterns are learned. A model may learn what experienced people call good without consistently choosing it. Learning a judgment is not the same as preferring it-or, more carefully, behaving consistently as though it prefers it. That may depend on the training objective.

Maybe fragments of taste are already present. The question is whether training can turn those fragments into stable judgment, and whose definition of good that judgment will represent.

But that does not remove the problem I am interested in. A model's taste must still be shaped by some signal: what is rewarded, whose preferences are represented, which contexts it has encountered, and what someone is trying to accomplish.

Even if models develop excellent judgment, humans still need enough judgment to choose the goal, recognise when the model is wrong, and take responsibility for the result.

Maybe the question is not whether AI can learn taste. It is what kind of taste it learns and what happens to ours while it does.

The Uncle Bob question

While thinking about this, I saw a post from Robert C. Martin, the author of Clean Code. He described not reading the code written by his agents and instead surrounding them with strong constraints: tests, quality metrics, coverage requirements, and other forms of verification.

What interested me was the experience behind the person choosing those constraints.

A recent exchange between John Carmack and Chris Lattner made this more concrete for me. Good building blocks and abstractions still matter, even when an agent writes the implementation. AI may explain the available trade-offs, but the remaining decision still belongs to someone. Perhaps recognising the important decision—and accepting responsibility for it—is part of technical taste.

An Anthropic team recently shared a practical example. They rewrote a Python API in Rust without having a Rust developer in the room. Claude wrote much of the implementation, while the humans designed the distributed system, planned the migration, and verified it by sending shadow traffic through both versions. Their expertise did not disappear; it moved from writing each line to defining the system and deciding what evidence would make it trustworthy.

That leaves the same question: if experience helps produce taste, can someone without it safely copy the workflow of someone who already has it?

Making work easier is not the problem. Removing the feedback loops through which people learn might be. We see what an experienced person can stop doing but ignore what they had to do before they could stop. We should automate repetition without automatically removing practice.

Manual and automatic cars

You do not need to drive a manual car to be a good driver. An automatic transmission removes work and makes driving accessible to more people.

But a manual car exposes part of the machine's behaviour. You feel the relationship between the engine, gears, speed, and movement. That does not make every manual driver a mechanic, but it provides feedback that an automatic system normally hides.

The lesson is not that everyone must suffer through the old way. It is that an abstraction may remove information along with effort. We need to know which information still matters and find another way to teach it.

Where creativity enters

Creativity and taste are related, but they are not the same.

Creativity generates possibilities. Taste chooses among them, combines them, and knows when to stop. Creativity asks, what else could this be? Taste asks, which version belongs here?

Problem-solving needs both. We frame the problem, generate possible solutions, test them, and refine what survives. Technical knowledge tells us what is possible. Creativity helps us escape the obvious answer. Taste helps us recognise the answer that fits.

Without creativity, taste can only criticise. Without taste, creativity can produce endlessly without knowing what deserves to remain.

What are we building towards?

I do not think anyone can confidently predict what the future will look like. We are building towards what we think it should be, and our tools will shape the people using them.

I do not think Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or anyone else building in this space can confidently predict that future either, even if their work is helping to usher in and shape a particular version of it.

The question may not be whether AI can do more of the work. It clearly can. The question is whether people will still develop the judgment needed to direct, evaluate, and take responsibility for that work.

I have a similar feeling when dealing with some non-critical, well-contained parts of Merdra. I do not need to hold every line in my head, but I need to understand what the system is doing and keep a mental map of it: how the parts relate, what assumptions they depend on, and where to look when something changes.

That distinction matters. Security, patient data, clinical safety, and other critical paths require much closer understanding and stronger verification. Abstraction may reduce how much code I read directly; it cannot remove my responsibility for knowing how those parts behave.

Maybe that is another form of taste: knowing how much detail can be abstracted away without surrendering understanding or responsibility.

These are questions without specific answers, at least for now.

Reviewers

Thanks to Rtrvl (CTO) and Fidel Etinosa for reviewing an early draft of this article.

entry.title: The Age of Infinite Software and Limited Imagination
entry.content:
We can build software faster than ever before.

You can describe an idea to an AI agent, give it a few instructions, and watch something that might have taken weeks or months begin taking shape in minutes.

You'd expect an explosion of creativity: more unusual ideas, ambitious experiments, and people attempting things that previously seemed impossible.

Yet sometimes I feel we're seeing the opposite.

Another AI wrapper. Another dashboard. Another application that looks remarkably similar to something that already exists.

Of course, people are doing genuinely interesting work. I'm not suggesting innovation has stopped. Maybe I'm just looking in the wrong places.

But I keep wondering:

If we now have some of the most powerful tools ever created, where is the spark?

Building isn't the same as imagining

There's a difference between being able to build something and imagining something worth building.

Generative AI is reducing the effort required to turn ideas into working systems. You don't necessarily need to understand every implementation detail before experimenting with an idea. That's incredible.

But making something easier to build doesn't automatically make us more imaginative. If we keep asking these systems to reproduce what already exists, why should we expect different outcomes?

I think we risk confusing productivity with creativity. Producing ten applications doesn't necessarily mean you've explored ten original ideas.

And perhaps that's where our thinking needs to change.

For a long time, much of our attention has gone into figuring out how to build things. As machines become increasingly capable of handling implementation, what happens to all that attention?

Do we simply produce more of the same things? Or do we start:

  • questioning assumptions,
  • connecting unrelated ideas, and
  • investigating problems we've accepted as normal?

What's stopping someone from vibe coding Google?

Here's something I've been thinking about.

What's stopping someone from opening Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent and asking it to build Google? They'd need:

  • a web crawler,
  • a search index,
  • a ranking algorithm,
  • a query interface, and
  • perhaps even an advertising system.

Nothing is stopping them from trying, and they could probably build a functional search engine prototype surprisingly quickly.

But have they built Google? Not quite.

Google isn't simply a collection of source files. Behind its search engine are enormous infrastructure investments, continuously updated indexes, ranking systems, years of operational knowledge, and an entire ecosystem.

Writing software that resembles Google is one problem. Building something capable of competing with it at scale is another.

Are software moats really disappearing?

This is why I find the argument that software moats are disappearing somewhat incomplete.

Yes, writing code is becoming cheaper. Some products will become much easier to replicate, and some existing advantages will weaken.

But the value of a system has never been entirely about how difficult its code is to write. These still matter:

  • reliability,
  • architecture,
  • distribution,
  • accumulated knowledge, and
  • the ability to operate under real-world conditions.

None of these advantages is permanent. AI might eventually make many of them easier to reproduce, too.

But making something easier to build doesn't necessarily make it easy to replace.

The obsession to keep pushing

There's something else I think matters enormously: obsession.

Not necessarily spending endless hours writing code yourself, but having an almost unreasonable desire to understand a problem and keep pushing a system beyond its limitations.

Imagine two people with access to exactly the same AI tools.

The first asks an agent to build an application. It works, so they launch it and move on.

The second keeps questioning everything:

  • Why does it work this way?
  • Why does this limitation exist?
  • What happens if we change the architecture?
  • Could we approach the entire problem differently?

Both have the same tools, but they might produce radically different outcomes.

You might no longer need to implement every component manually, but you can still be the person directing the experiments, questioning the results, and deciding what to try next. And I find that fascinating.

Instead of spending weeks implementing a single approach, you might be able to investigate several alternatives, discover why they fail, and keep refining your understanding.

Of course, obsession alone isn't enough. You can spend years perfecting something nobody needs. But combine it with curiosity, technical understanding, judgment, and a willingness to experiment, and there's still something valuable there.

The first working implementation shouldn't necessarily be the end of your imagination. Sometimes it's where the interesting questions begin.

This goes beyond software

I don't think this opportunity is limited to software. Think about hardware, robotics, energy, manufacturing, or scientific research.

Imagine designing a robotic hand. You describe what you want, use AI to explore mechanical designs, simulate their movements, and generate components for a prototype. Eventually, you build one.

It works, but it struggles to pick up a tiny screw.

What happens next?

Do you accept the limitation, or do you start questioning the finger geometry, sensors, materials, and control system? Perhaps an entirely different mechanism would work better.

AI could help you investigate those possibilities, but someone still has to recognise the problem, test the ideas, and understand what the results mean.

And unlike software, the physical world has constraints that don't disappear because an AI generated a convincing design. Materials cost money. Components wear out. Manufacturing takes time. Physics doesn't care how impressive your prompt is.

Still, as these tools improve, individuals and smaller teams may gain the ability to attempt increasingly complex projects. There are machines we haven't invented, systems we haven't connected, and problems we haven't investigated deeply enough.

Not everything has to become another application.

A forced evolution in how we think?

I sometimes wonder whether we're approaching a point where a kind of forced evolution in our thinking becomes necessary. Not biological evolution, but a change in how we approach problems.

We've spent years learning how to use computers to accomplish tasks. Now computers are beginning to handle increasingly complex tasks on our behalf.

Perhaps this means we need to become more deliberate about exercising our creativity and logical reasoning: to ask better questions, challenge assumptions, and understand systems rather than merely operate them. To see possibilities where others see limitations.

I'm not suggesting that implementation no longer matters, or that technical understanding becomes irrelevant. Quite the opposite.

The better you understand something, the more effectively you can question it. And the more capable our tools become, the further those questions might take us.

But there's another possibility worth considering.

What if increasingly capable AI makes it easier for us to avoid thinking altogether?

We could become so comfortable accepting generated solutions that we stop investigating why they work, whether they're correct, or whether a better approach exists.

I don't think that's inevitable. But it's a choice we'll increasingly have to make.

Where is the spark?

There is still so much left to solve: healthcare, energy, robotics, biology, computing, and countless problems we probably haven't even recognised yet.

I don't think we're running out of ideas. I think we might be underestimating how much remains possible.

And perhaps the opportunity presented by generative AI isn't simply to build the same things faster. It's to explore things we previously couldn't afford to attempt.

We've made it easier than ever to turn an idea into something real. Maybe it's time we became more ambitious about the ideas themselves.

The machines are getting better at building. Are we getting better at imagining?

entry.title: Two mind blowing articles i read today
entry.content:
Articles on Startups and Success

  • How To Be Successful

  • Hard Startups


How to be successful :

Everyone has a different definition of success, irrespective of those beliefs we all do have a specific goal in mind that is to be successful. Meaning we do all have to put in the hard work, sleepless night and also working smart.

Sam altman actually explained, so I won't go into full details you can always read the articles.

Self belief: Not believing in yourself makes the whole process even harder, this made me remember one of steve job's quote..

"The people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world are the one who do."


Learning to think independently: There is always a solution to every problem, success is actually 99% failure and 1% success, one thing i learn to do is treat every failed attempt as an experiment or a learning process...


Focus:
This is one of the quality i currently lack, According to Steve Jobs,

“People think focus means saying yes to the thing you've got to focus on. But that's not what it means at all. It means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. You have to pick carefully. I'm actually as proud of the things we haven't done as the things I have done."


Others i consider important

  • becoming hard to compete with
  • be bold
  • be internally driven
  • Taking risks
  • be good at sales
  • build a network
  • You get rich by owning things

Hard startups

Everyone has a different perspective to this, I like the writer's perspective and also belief startup founders should have a long-term commitment. This made me curious what should startup in developing countries focus on...?

entry.title: Technological Innovation in developing countries
entry.content:
Note: These are based on my views on factors affecting the rate of innovation in developing countries. I might be wrong, but at the same time, I might be right.

Writing this article feels a little weird for me; it seems like something I should not write about, but I also have the feeling that I should do it anyway. Keeping this as short as possible, I won't be able to cover all areas.

People in developing countries seem to believe that the governing entities are solely responsible for bringing about technological innovation (this is done indirectly), which is something I strongly disagree with. I guess I am not expressing this in the right way; coming from a tech background, there is a lot I don't fully understand about politics. It's not an excuse, but rather than complaining, that energy should be directed towards something else.

Secondly, the mindset (culture) and beliefs of the people are really mind-blowing. I love this quote: "You are what you believe in." It's really funny how, at the age of 20-25 in most cases, you are still considered incapable of making decisions that could cause a serious change in society, down to individual families, and this becomes a loop.

It makes me wonder what the adults spend their youthful age doing in their 20's....??? This makes me want to give examples of Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg...

To a point, you can't entirely blame society for this; many youths spend their time in the most unproductive ways you could ever think of, involving themselves in internet fraud and other criminal activities, etc.

There is a lot at play here:

  1. Lack of knowledge, even in a major field (poor education background, mostly outdated curriculum).
  2. Lack of infrastructure, etc.

Technological innovation can be brought about by innovative individuals (Tech Visionaries) who:

x. See things differently.
x. Have a serious, intense passion for what they do.
x. Are ready to take action no matter the odds.
x. Are tired of doing things the old way (with low outcomes).
x. Are highly curious (question everything) and have the ability to connect the dots.

Don't get me wrong, one person can't actually change the world; you are going to work together with intelligent humans and people who think alike to actually make a mark.
